Thank you. I found Q3.4 challenging because tracking online activity feels invasive. I believe the group was right to largely reject it.

I think Q5.2 about fairness is crucial. The consensus on prioritizing equal recall across groups is important—it ensures we don't overlook students who need support, even if it means contacting a few more who don't.

On data privacy (Q3.5), the group was split on nationality and disability. I lean toward using sensitive data like disability only if it significantly improves fairness. Some may argue that certain data types could help marginalized groups, but I worry about potential misuse or unintended consequences.

Overall, transparency (Q4) is key to maintaining trust, even if it means identifying fewer students initially.

I found Q3.4 particularly difficult because I understand the need for comprehensive data to help identify students early, but tracking online activity feels like crossing a privacy boundary.

I think Q5.1 and Q5.2 are crucial—they directly address how fairly the model treats different student groups. The group’s strong preference for equal recall is reassuring, as it aligns with ensuring no one slips through the cracks.

On data use (Q3), I was surprised by how many were open to using nationality or disability information, even if only to improve fairness. While I see the rationale—helping marginalized groups—I worry about misuse or unintended consequences. Maybe an opt-out could help balance privacy concerns and support needs?

Transparency is key. Explainability matters for trust, but some trade-offs might be acceptable if it means reaching more students in need.
